title: Why Krishna keeps working
hookLine: a king who reached the highest goal without leaving the palace
carry: lokasangraha: act to hold the world together
tomorrow: Taught to the sun, told again

lines: JANAKA: A KING AND A SAGE.
cards: Janaka was a king. He had a palace, a court, a kingdom to run: taxes, quarrels, harvests.
Two days ago we watched the sage Yajnavalkya tell him he'd reached fearlessness, and the Hindu tradition remembers him that way, a sage who knew the Self while sitting on a throne.
Halfway through chapter three, Krishna reaches for his name. Janaka and others like him, he says, reached perfection through action itself. Not by walking away.
By doing the work. Then Krishna names someone else who never stops working: himself.

teach.b: The word is lokasangraha. Loka is the world, the people in it. Sangraha is a holding together, a gathering.
Krishna tells Arjuna to act with that in view. Then he gives a very human reason.

teach.h: WHAT A LEADER DOES, OTHERS FOLLOW.
teach.b: Whatever a leading person does, others do too. Whatever standard they set, the world follows. So the way you work isn't private.
Somebody is watching. Then Krishna points at himself.

teach.h: KRISHNA NEEDS NOTHING, AND STILL ACTS.
teach.b: There's nothing in the three worlds, he says, that I have to do, nothing I lack, nothing to gain. And yet I keep acting. If I stopped, people everywhere would follow my path, and the worlds would fall apart.
So the wise should act without attachment, as the unwise act with it, for the sake of holding the world together.
And they shouldn't unsettle the minds of people attached to their work; let them keep working, and show them how by example.
A few verses later: better one's own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's done well. Your own place in the holding-together, even if it's clumsy. Commentators weigh this differently.
Shankara, who holds that liberation finally comes through knowledge, reads the call to act here as fitting for those still on the way, and as an example for others.

Some modern readers took lokasangraha as close to the heart of the whole Gita. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, in his long commentary called the Gita Rahasya, read it that way, as a charge to keep working for the world's welfare.
The verses can carry both. Either way, karma here isn't only my action.
It's one thread in a cloth that a lot of other people are wearing.

how: Some Hindus who study the Gita point to King Janaka as the model of a person who lives in the world and knows the Self, and some study circles dwell on the verse on one's own dharma (3.35).

o: work that matters only to the one who is doing it
action done for the holding together of the world
a king's duty to collect taxes and settle quarrels

games.q: Gita, chapter three, second half — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna says he acts because he has something left to gain
he says there's nothing he needs or lacks, and still he acts.
Krishna tells the wise to shake up people attached to their work
he says not to unsettle their minds, but to show by example.
Tilak read lokasangraha as a charge to keep working for the world's welfare
in his commentary, the Gita Rahasya.

games.q: you're Krishna. you need nothing and lack nothing. why keep acting?
o: because people follow what you do, and the worlds would fall apart.
games.why: Krishna says that if he stopped, people would follow his path and the worlds would fall apart. so the wise act for lokasangraha, holding the world together.

practice: Bring to mind the people who see how you work, a child, a coworker, a younger sibling, a neighbor, and just notice that they're there.
Then take one thing you do every day, the dishes, a meeting, a commute, and ask what it teaches without a word, seeing it as one thread in the cloth. If you pray, you can offer that one thread.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action done for lokasangraha, the holding together of the world, the way King Janaka did it, and the way Krishna says he does.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: lokasangraha, from loka, world, and sangraha, holding together. Gita 3.20 and 3.25.

carryVoice: Your line: lokasangraha: act to hold the world together. Tomorrow, a teaching with a family tree. Day nine hundred sixty-four, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.20–3.26 (Janaka; lokasangraha; what the best do, others follow; Krishna acts though he needs nothing; do not unsettle the attached)
Bhagavad Gita 3.35 (better one's own dharma, though imperfect)
